I. Beta-Lactams

pp. 1–5

A. Penicillin — architecture, action, and molecular mimicry

  • Penicillin is a cell-wall synthesis inhibitor used mainly against Gram-positive bacteria.
  • The bactericidal activity depends on the intact β-lactam ring, fused to a thiazolidine ring in the 6-aminopenicillanic acid nucleus.
  • Side-chain modification changes properties and allows production of semisynthetic penicillins.
1D-Ala-D-Ala mimicryβ-Lactam resembles the terminal peptide substrate.
2PBP bindingPBP recognizes the mimic and forms a stable covalent complex.
3Cross-linking failsTranspeptidation stops and the wall progressively weakens.
4Autolysis continuesAutolysins keep degrading existing peptidoglycan.
5Osmotic lysisThe weakened cell swells, bursts, and dies.
Mechanistic cueβ-Lactams work best against actively dividing bacteria because those organisms are actively synthesizing cell wall.
Figures 2–3, p. 2. Structural mimicry of D-Ala-D-Ala leads to covalent PBP inhibition, loss of cross-linking, continued autolysis, then osmotic lysis. Click to enlarge.

Penicillin classification anchors

  • Natural: Penicillin G IV, Penicillin V oral and acid-stable.
  • Antistaphylococcal: Nafcillin, oxacillin, dicloxacillin. Bulky side chains provide a steric shield against staphylococcal penicillinases. They cover MSSA, not MRSA.
  • Extended spectrum: Ampicillin, amoxicillin, piperacillin. Coverage improves for Gram-negative rods. Piperacillin targets Pseudomonas.
  • β-Lactamase inhibitor partners: Clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam.

Penicillin kinetics and toxicities

  • Renal clearance: about 10% glomerular filtration and 90% active tubular secretion. Typical half-life is under 1 hour.
  • Probenecid: blocks active tubular secretion and prolongs penicillin levels.
  • Biliary exceptions: nafcillin is mainly biliary. Oxacillin uses renal and biliary routes.
  • Major adverse effect: hypersensitivity from rash to anaphylactic shock, stated as about 0.05% in the lecture.
  • Very high doses: seizures, confusion, encephalopathy, especially with renal dysfunction.
  • Specific toxicity: nafcillin neutropenia, oxacillin hepatitis, methicillin acute interstitial nephritis.

Four biochemical strategies to evade β-lactams

Destroy the drug

β-Lactamases hydrolyze the β-lactam ring and generate inactive products.

Change the target

Low-affinity PBPs. Classic lecture examples are PBP2a in MRSA encoded by mecA and altered PBPs in resistant S. pneumoniae.

Keep the drug out

Loss or mutation of Gram-negative porins impairs penetration.

Pump the drug out

Active multidrug efflux pumps lower periplasmic drug concentrations.

B. Cephalosporins

  • Semi-synthetic bactericidal cell-wall inhibitors derived from Acremonium chrysogenum.
  • Contain a β-lactam ring fused to a dihydrothiazine ring.
  • MOA parallels penicillin through PBPs, transpeptidase inhibition, autolysis, and cell-wall deficiency.
  • Resistance includes altered transpeptidase affinity or structure, β-lactamase production, and reduced permeability.

Ceftriaxone: bilirubin displacement with neonatal kernicterus risk and calcium precipitation causing biliary pseudolithiasis.
MTT side chain: cefotetan and cefamandole can cause hypoprothrombinemia and a disulfiram-like alcohol reaction.
Appendix Figure 6, p. 29. Lecturer cephalosporin generation summary referenced from the lesson. Click to enlarge.

C. Monobactam

  • Monocyclic β-lactams. The β-lactam ring is not fused to another ring.
  • Agents listed include aztreonam, tigemonam, carumonam, and nocardicin.
  • Activity is restricted to aerobic Gram-negative bacteria, including Neisseria and Pseudomonas.
  • Aztreonam is useful for Gram-negative coverage in severe penicillin allergy because cross-allergenicity is absent with penicillins and cephalosporins, with the lecture exception of ceftazidime because of an identical side chain.
  • Resistance mechanisms include altered transpeptidases and β-lactamases.

D. Carbapenem

  • Among the broadest-spectrum β-lactams and reserved for serious or resistant infections.
  • Group 1: ertapenem. Group 2: imipenem, meropenem, doripenem.
  • Imipenem is hydrolyzed by renal dihydropeptidase-1 and is co-administered with cilastatin.
  • Meropenem, doripenem, and ertapenem are stable to that enzyme and do not require cilastatin.
  • Ertapenem lacks activity against Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter.
  • All are renally cleared and require dose reduction in renal insufficiency.
Imipenem warningSeizure risk rises with high doses and renal failure. The lecture attributes neurotoxicity to competition with GABA binding. Discontinue if seizure develops.

β-Lactamase inhibitors

  • Clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam are suicide inhibitors structurally related to β-lactams with weak intrinsic antibacterial activity.
  • They covalently and irreversibly inactivate susceptible serine β-lactamases, especially class A plasmid-mediated enzymes.
  • Clinical combinations highlighted: amoxicillin-clavulanate, ampicillin-sulbactam, and piperacillin-tazobactam.

II. Glycopeptides and Miscellaneous Cell-Wall / Membrane Agents

pp. 5–7

A. Vancomycin

Target and mechanism

  • Large, water-soluble tricyclic glycopeptide active against Gram-positive bacteria.
  • Cannot traverse narrow Gram-negative outer-membrane porins.
  • Unlike β-lactams, it does not inhibit PBPs.
  • Binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of nascent peptidoglycan and forms five hydrogen bonds.
  • Sterically blocks transglycosylation and transpeptidation during late extracellular wall assembly.

Resistance

  • VRE / VRSA: terminal target substitution to D-Ala-D-Lac or D-Ala-D-Ser.
  • D-Ala-D-Lac removes a crucial hydrogen bond and lowers affinity by about 1,000-fold.
  • VISA: thickened wall with excess nonfunctional D-Ala-D-Ala targets that sequester vancomycin.

PK and clinical use

  • Poor oral absorption means systemic MRSA infections require IV vancomycin.
  • Oral vancomycin is reserved for C. difficile colitis because it remains in the gut.
  • About 90% is cleared by glomerular filtration.
  • Lecture TDM target for severe MRSA: 15–20 mcg/mL trough.

Adverse effects

  • Infusion-related flushing and erythematous rash from direct mast-cell histamine release.
  • Not a true allergy. It is rate-dependent and can be prevented by slow 1–2 hour infusion or antihistamines.
  • Dose-related AKI risk increases with high troughs, renal dysfunction, and other nephrotoxins.
  • Ototoxicity is less common and may be irreversible.
Kinetic exceptionsMost β-lactams are rapidly renally cleared.
Nafcillin, oxacillin, and ceftriaxone are lecture-highlighted biliary exceptions.
Vancomycin is mostly filtered by the kidney and requires monitoring.

B. Oritavancin

  • Newer glycopeptide that blocks transglycosylation and transpeptidation.
  • Focused on Gram-positive organisms including resistant strains.
  • Lecture notes activity against VRS and VRE.
  • Phase IV trial mentioned for skin, soft-tissue, and MRSA infections.

C. Teicoplanin

  • Mechanistically similar to vancomycin with D-Ala-D-Ala binding.
  • Bactericidal against Gram-positive organisms including MRSA and MRSE.
  • Lecture half-life: about 70–100 hours, enabling dosing every 3–4 days.
  • Indications include endocarditis, bone and joint infection, bacteremia, pneumonia, skin and soft-tissue infection, β-lactam allergy, and oral use for C. difficile.
  • Adverse effects resemble glycopeptides: rash, fever, nephrotoxicity, rare ototoxicity.

III. Protein Inhibitors Overview

p. 7

A. Selective toxicity: why bacterial ribosomes are drug targets

  • Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, made of 30S + 50S.
  • Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, made of 40S + 60S.
  • This structural separation permits selective ribosomal binding at therapeutic concentrations.
  • Mitochondria also have 70S-like ribosomes, which the lecture uses to explain toxicity from some ribosomal inhibitors during prolonged or high-dose exposure.
Must KnowBuy AT 30, CELL for 50
AT: Aminoglycosides and Tetracyclines → 30S.
CELL: Chloramphenicol, Erythromycin, Linezolid, Lincosamides → 50S.
30S versus 50S targets
TargetClassBinding behaviorCore effect
30STetracyclinesReversibleBlocks aminoacyl-tRNA access to the A-site → bacteriostatic
30SAminoglycosidesIrreversibleMisreading, abnormal proteins, membrane damage → bactericidal
50S / 23SMacrolidesReversibleBlocks translocation and exit-tunnel transit → bacteriostatic
50S / 23SLincosamidesOverlapping locus with macrolidesTranslocation arrest → bacteriostatic
50SChloramphenicolReversibleDirect peptidyl transferase blockade → usually bacteriostatic
50S / 23SLinezolidInitiation-phase targetPrevents functional 70S initiation-complex assembly → bacteriostatic

Early translation at 16S rRNA

Tetracycline

Reversible and static. The drug binds conserved 16S rRNA on 30S, excludes aminoacyl-tRNA from the A-site, and stops elongation without directly killing the cell.

Aminoglycoside

Cationic and lethal. Entry requires aerobic energy-dependent transport. Binding near the A-site produces codon misreading and abnormal proteins that damage the membrane.

23S rRNA and the 50S subunit

  • Macrolides + lincosamides: bind near the peptidyl transferase center and halt translocation. Their binding sites overlap.
  • Chloramphenicol: directly inhibits peptidyl transferase and prevents peptide-bond formation.
  • Oxazolidinones: suppress 70S initiation-complex assembly and stop synthesis at the earliest phase.

IV. Tetracyclines

pp. 8–9

A. Overview

  • Broad-spectrum bacteriostatic drugs first isolated from Actinomycetes.
  • Examples: tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, tigecycline.
  • Useful against atypical organisms including Chlamydia, Rickettsia, and some spirochetes.
  • The lecture highlights doxycycline prophylaxis for leptospirosis.
Classification by duration
DurationAgents
Short, 6–8 hTetracycline, chlortetracycline, oxytetracycline
Intermediate, 12 hDemeclocycline, methacycline
Long, 16–18 hDoxycycline, minocycline, tigecycline

B. Tetracycline translation arrest

Step 1Entry and accumulationPassive diffusion plus active concentration in susceptible bacteria.
Step 230S bindingReversible attachment to 30S near the A-site.
Step 3tRNA exclusionAminoacyl-tRNA cannot associate with the acceptor site.
Step 4Translation stopNo new amino acids are added. Growth and replication are suppressed.

C. Resistance genetics

Efflux

Tet(A–E) in Gram-negative organisms and Tet(K) in staphylococci reduce intracellular drug levels. Tigecycline resists export by standard older pumps.

Ribosomal protection

Tet(M) binds the ribosome and dislodges tetracycline so translation can continue.

Other lecture mechanisms

Reduced entry, ribosomal mutations, and monooxygenase-mediated hydroxylation can also produce resistance.

Overcoming resistanceTigecycline is a semisynthetic glycylcycline with a bulky side chain that helps evade standard efflux and Tet(M)-mediated protection.

D. Clinical profile and safety

Clinical landmarks

  • Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia, Rickettsia
  • Vibrio cholerae, plague, tularemia, brucellosis
  • Spirochetes including Lyme disease
  • Doxycycline and minocycline are well absorbed orally.
  • Doxycycline is eliminated mainly non-renally in feces and does not require renal adjustment in the lecture.
  • Tigecycline is IV-only for complicated skin and soft-tissue infections.

Safety anchors

  • Chelates Ca, Mg, Fe, Al → impaired absorption with dairy, antacids, iron.
  • Binds developing bone and teeth → brown enamel discoloration and inhibited bone growth.
  • Avoid in pregnancy, lactation, and children under 8.
  • GI upset, esophageal ulcer, photosensitivity, hepatic toxicity, superinfection.
  • Demeclocycline: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

V. Macrolides and Ketolides

p. 9

Macrolide structure and mechanism

  • Large 14-, 15-, or 16-membered macrocyclic lactone rings attached to deoxy sugars.
  • Class members highlighted: erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin.
  • Bind reversibly to bases on 23S rRNA of 50S.
  • Obstruct the peptide exit tunnel and prevent peptidyl-tRNA translocation from the A-site to the P-site.
  • Result: bacteriostatic elongation arrest.
  • Macrolides, lincosamides, and streptogramins have overlapping sites, explaining simultaneous cross-resistance in the lecture.

A. Safety and dynamics

Pharmacokinetic highlights

  • Erythromycin base is acid-labile and needs enteric coating or stable salt formulations.
  • Clarithromycin and azithromycin are acid-stable with better oral absorption and tissue levels.
  • Azithromycin half-life: 68 hours in the lecture, allowing short 3-day courses.
  • Macrolides concentrate in bile and are cleared mainly in feces. Clarithromycin requires renal adjustment.

Interaction and safety

  • Erythromycin + clarithromycin inhibit CYP3A4 and can raise statin, warfarin, and theophylline levels.
  • Azithromycin avoids this CYP3A4 interaction pattern in the lecture.
  • High concentrations can block cardiac hERG potassium channels → QTc prolongation and torsades de pointes.
  • Erythromycin estolate can cause cholestatic jaundice.
  • Erythromycin stimulates motilin receptors and commonly causes severe GI upset.

Ketolide evolution

  • Telithromycin was developed to improve potency against resistant organisms.
  • A 3-keto group replaces the standard L-cladinose sugar.
  • High-affinity binding at two 50S sites provides greater potency against resistant strains.
  • Use is restricted by severe hepatotoxicity. The lecture limits its niche to community-acquired pneumonia.

VI. Clindamycin

pp. 9–10

A. MOA and clinical roles

  • Binds the 50S exit tunnel at a site overlapping macrolide and streptogramin targets.
  • Inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis and can suppress production of bacterial superantigen exotoxins.
  • The lecture highlights severe toxin-mediated streptococcal and staphylococcal disease such as necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock syndrome.
  • Inhibits synthesis of staphylococcal M-protein, which the lecture links to improved phagocytosis.
Clinical niches
NicheLecture point
AnaerobesStrong activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative anaerobes, including B. fragilis and Prevotella.
Above the diaphragmAspiration pneumonia, lung abscesses, deep oral infections.
Bone and jointExcellent tissue penetration and usefulness in osteomyelitis.
CSFDoes not cross the BBB into CSF.
Necrotizing fasciitisLecture describes empiric combination with vancomycin and a β-lactamase inhibitor.
Black box warningPseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridioides difficile is the major toxicity.
Clindamycin suppresses protective gut flora → resistant C. difficile overgrows → exotoxins damage mucosa → fibrin, inflammatory cells, and necrotic debris form pseudomembranes.
The lecture emphasizes reserving clindamycin for serious infections where alternatives are not appropriate.

VII. Chloramphenicol

p. 10

A. Overview

  • Originally obtained from Streptomyces venezuelae. Now synthetic.
  • Broad-spectrum and usually bacteriostatic, with bactericidal activity at high concentration or in selected sensitive organisms.
  • Excellent tissue and CSF penetration. Crosses placenta and is secreted in bile and milk.
  • Because of serious toxicity, the lecture frames it as a drug of last resort when safer alternatives are unavailable.

B. Core mechanism and resistance

  • Binds reversibly near the peptidyl transferase center of the 50S subunit.
  • Directly prevents peptide-bond formation and freezes translation.
  • Bactericidal exceptions named: H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae.
  • Resistance: R-plasmid encoded acetyltransferase, target-affinity change, or decreased penetration.
Must KnowHost mitochondrial inhibition drives the classic toxicity triad: bone marrow suppression, aplastic anemia, and gray baby syndrome.
C. Chloramphenicol toxicities
ToxicityMechanism / defining featureClinical consequence
Bone marrow suppressionDose-dependent and reversible inhibition of host mitochondrial ribosomesAnemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia that resolves after stopping the drug
Idiosyncratic aplastic anemiaRare, unpredictable, unrelated to dose or therapy lengthIrreversible, often fatal, can appear weeks to months after therapy and may progress to leukemia
Gray baby syndromeNeonatal deficiency of functional UDP-glucuronyl transferase → failed metabolism and toxic accumulationGray skin, blue lips, limp tone, circulatory collapse, high mortality

VIII. Linezolid (Zyvox)

pp. 10–11

Core profile

  • Completely synthetic oxazolidinone.
  • Mainly targets resistant Gram-positive organisms, including MRSA and VRE.
  • Also active against Streptococcus pneumoniae. No clinically significant Gram-negative coverage in the lecture.
  • 100% oral bioavailability allows easy IV-to-PO conversion.
  • Adults: 600 mg IV/PO every 12 h. Typical lecture duration: 10–14 days depending on infection.

A. Oxazolidinone initiation blockade

Step 123S targetingLinezolid binds a specific 23S rRNA pocket on 50S.
Step 2Initiation blockade30S and 50S cannot properly assemble with initiator tRNA into a functional 70S complex.
Step 3Translation cannot startProtein synthesis is halted at the earliest phase.
Step 4Clinical effectPurely bacteriostatic growth inhibition in the lecture.

B. Safety and interactions

  • Myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia with therapy beyond 2 weeks. CBC and platelet monitoring are emphasized.
  • Long-term use: peripheral neuropathy, irreversible optic neuropathy, and lactic acidosis.
  • Linezolid is a reversible nonselective inhibitor of MAO-A and MAO-B.
  • SSRIs and other serotonergic antidepressants can precipitate potentially lethal serotonin syndrome.
  • Lecture advises avoiding tyramine-rich foods.
Clinical pearlExcellent oral alternative to IV vancomycin for selected MRSA pneumonia or VRE infections, but prolonged therapy is limited by hematologic and neurologic toxicity.

IX. Aminoglycosides

pp. 11–15

A. Overview and chemistry

  • Rapidly bactericidal, especially against aerobic Gram-negative organisms.
  • Main agents: gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, streptomycin, neomycin and related drugs.
  • First aminoglycoside taught: streptomycin, discovered in 1943 from Actinomycetes.
  • Central hexose nucleus plus amino sugars. Streptomycin uses streptidine. Gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin use 2-deoxystreptamine.
  • Many basic amino groups make aminoglycosides highly polar, positively charged, water-soluble, and poor at crossing lipid membranes.
  • Activity improves in alkaline conditions and falls in acidic infected tissue and abscesses.
Appendix Figure 10, p. 30. Structural chemistry and pH / solubility consequences. Click to enlarge.

B–D. Three-phase uptake and 30S translation blockade

Phase 1Outer-membrane diffusionHydrophilic drug crosses Gram-negative porins into the periplasm. No active energy is required.
Phase 2Energy-dependent entryInner-membrane transport requires oxygen and the proton motive force.
30S targetInitiation blockadeInterferes with formation of the active 70S initiation complex.
30S targetmRNA misreadingWrong amino acids are incorporated into aberrant proteins.
30S targetPolysome breakupTranslocation is disrupted and polysomes break into nonfunctional monosomes.
Lethal loopMembrane damageAberrant proteins damage membrane integrity, allowing still more aminoglycoside entry.
Why no anaerobic activity?Oxygen-dependent transport is required.
Strict anaerobes cannot support the active entry step.
Abscesses and necrotic low-oxygen tissue also impede uptake.
Appendix Figure 11, p. 30. Entry, oxygen-dependent transport, 30S binding, miscoding, membrane injury, bactericidal effect. Click to enlarge.

E. Penicillin–aminoglycoside synergy

  • Cell-wall active drugs such as penicillins, cephalosporins, and vancomycin weaken the peptidoglycan barrier.
  • This increases aminoglycoside penetration and produces enhanced bacterial killing that the lecture describes as true synergy.
  • Important niches include deep-seated infections such as enterococcal or staphylococcal endocarditis and serious Pseudomonas infection.
  • The lecture also notes that non-aminoglycoside combinations may be preferred in some enterococcal endocarditis cases to avoid renal damage.
Must Know“Penicillin opens the door, aminoglycosides enter to attack.”
This does not mean the combination is automatically preferred. Always account for toxicity, especially nephrotoxicity.
Appendix Figure 12, p. 31. The lecturer’s synergy figure. Click to enlarge.

F. Bacterial biochemical escapes

1. Enzymatic modification

The most important clinical mechanism. R-plasmid transferases add chemical groups:

  • AAC acetylation
  • APH phosphorylation
  • ANT adenylation

Modified drug loses 30S binding. Amikacin and plazomicin are designed to resist many modifying enzymes.

2. Decreased penetration

Porin loss impairs passive entry. Electron-transport or proton-motive-force disruption blocks active energy-dependent transport.

3. Ribosomal target change

Mutations can alter or delete the 30S receptor or shift the binding site, lowering aminoglycoside affinity. The lecture highlights this in streptomycin monotherapy.

I. Strategic dosing

Concentration-dependent killing

  • Higher peak above MIC produces greater bacterial killing.
  • Critical relationship: Cmax / MIC.
  • Gentamicin and tobramycin peak target for serious Gram-negative bacteremia in the lecture: 8–10 mcg/mL.

Post-antibiotic effect

  • Suppression persists after the serum level falls below MIC.
  • Lecture duration against susceptible Gram-negative organisms: 2–6 hours.
  • Persistent ribosomal injury helps explain the effect.
Once-daily logicHigh peak, low trough.
A large dose maximizes concentration-dependent killing.
PAE continues suppression as the serum level falls.
An 18–24 hour washout period reduces tissue accumulation and toxicity.

Continuous trough associated with severe toxicity

Appendix Figure 14, p. 32. Once-daily dosing, PAE, trough threshold, and TDM. Click to enlarge.

J. Excretion dynamics and renal impairment

  • Aminoglycosides are cleared strictly by the kidneys. Excretion tracks GFR / creatinine clearance.
  • Normal half-life: 2–3 h. Severe renal impairment can extend it to 24–48 h.
  • Hemodialysis removes only part of the drug, stated as 40–60% for gentamicin. Peritoneal dialysis is even less effective.
  • Once-daily dosing is avoided if CrCl <60 mL/min. If GFR is above 60 mL/min, the lecture considers 5–7 mg/kg once daily safe.
  • Traditional renal adjustment can either lengthen the dosing interval or reduce the dose while keeping the interval.
Must KnowBefore giving an aminoglycoside, know the patient’s renal function and keep monitoring it during therapy.

K. Major adverse effects

Aminoglycoside toxicity
ToxicityMechanism / patternHigh-yield anchors
NephrotoxicityRenal cortical and proximal tubular accumulation → lysosomal swelling, rupture, cell damageReversible AKI in 5–25% after systemic therapy beyond 3–5 days. Neomycin, tobramycin, gentamicin are most nephrotoxic in the lecture. Rising trough can precede rising creatinine.
OtotoxicityProgressive destruction of inner-ear hair cellsIrreversible. Auditory: neomycin, kanamycin, amikacin. Vestibular: streptomycin, gentamicin. Risk rises after >5 days, older age, low GFR. Loop diuretics amplify risk.
Neuromuscular blockadePresynaptic calcium-channel blockade reduces calcium-dependent ACh releaseHigh doses can cause curare-like weakness and respiratory paralysis. Calcium gluconate first-line antidote in the lecture. Neostigmine second-line. Strictly contraindicated in myasthenia gravis.

IX-L. Spectinomycin

p. 15

Related aminocyclitol alternative for resistant gonorrhea

  • Aminocyclitol structurally related to aminoglycosides, but lacks amino sugars and glycosidic bonds.
  • Binds reversibly to 30S and inhibits protein synthesis.
  • Unlike aminoglycosides, reversible binding makes it bacteriostatic, not bactericidal.
  • Shows no cross-resistance with other major anti-gonorrheal agents in the lecture.
  • Used almost exclusively as an alternative for drug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae or severe penicillin / cephalosporin allergy.
  • Not recommended for pharyngeal gonorrhea because of poor efficacy and high failure rates.
  • Single IM dose 2–4 g. Injection pain, fever, nausea are common. Nephrotoxicity and anemia are extremely rare.

X. Antimetabolites and Nucleic Acid Synthesis Inhibitors — Therapeutic Targets Only

pp. 15–16 + Appendix p. 32
Scope noteThis tab includes only the Section X target overview that appears before XI.
Detailed sulfonamide, trimethoprim, folate-metabolism, resistance, clinical-use, and toxicity content from XI. Antifolate Drugs is intentionally excluded.

Two routes to stop microbial replication

Folate pathway antagonists

  • Bacteria must synthesize tetrahydrofolate de novo to make purines and DNA.
  • Sulfonamides mimic PABA and inhibit dihydropteroate synthase.
  • Trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase.
  • The lecture target overview states that paired sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim creates sequential blockade, converting individual bacteriostatic effects into a powerful bactericidal combination.

Fluoroquinolone nucleic-acid blockade

  • Targets bacterial enzymes controlling DNA supercoiling and chromosome separation.
  • Inhibits DNA gyrase / topoisomerase II and topoisomerase IV.
  • Trapping the DNA-enzyme cleavage complex produces double-stranded DNA breaks.
  • The lecture describes the result as rapidly bactericidal.

Cram Sheet

Sections I–X only
Core mechanisms
  • β-Lactam: D-Ala-D-Ala mimic → covalent PBP inhibition → no peptidoglycan cross-linking → autolysis continues → osmotic lysis.
  • Vancomycin: binds D-Ala-D-Ala itself → blocks transglycosylation + transpeptidation. VRE changes the terminus to D-Ala-D-Lac or D-Ser.
  • Tetracycline: reversible 30S A-site block → no aminoacyl-tRNA entry → bacteriostatic.
  • Aminoglycoside: oxygen-dependent entry → irreversible 30S binding → miscoding + abnormal membrane proteins → bactericidal.
  • Macrolide / clindamycin: 50S exit-tunnel / translocation arrest.
  • Chloramphenicol: 50S peptidyl transferase block.
  • Linezolid: 23S rRNA → prevents 70S initiation-complex formation.
Memory anchors
Lecture mnemonicBuy AT 30, CELL for 50
AT = Aminoglycosides + Tetracyclines.
CELL = Chloramphenicol + Erythromycin + Linezolid + Lincosamides.
Aminoglycoside synergyPenicillin opens the door, aminoglycosides enter to attack.
Cell-wall damage improves aminoglycoside penetration.
Do not assume the combination is automatically preferred because renal toxicity still matters.
If you see X → think Y
MRSA + cephalosporinThink 5th generation ceftaroline and PBP2a affinity.
Severe penicillin allergy + aerobic Gram-negativeThink aztreonam. Remember the ceftazidime side-chain exception.
ImipenemThink cilastatin, renal DHP-1, and seizure risk.
Oral vancomycinThink C. difficile colitis, because it stays in the gut.
Clindamycin + severe diarrheaThink C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis.
Newborn + chloramphenicolThink gray baby syndrome from immature glucuronidation.
Linezolid + SSRIThink serotonin syndrome.
Aminoglycoside + anaerobeThink no activity because oxygen-dependent transport is required.
Myasthenia gravis + aminoglycosideThink dangerous neuromuscular blockade.

Resistance shortcuts
  • β-Lactam: destroy drug, change target, keep drug out, pump drug out.
  • Vancomycin: change D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac / D-Ser or thicken wall.
  • Tetracycline: Tet efflux + Tet(M) ribosomal protection, plus reduced entry / target mutation / inactivation.
  • Chloramphenicol: acetyltransferase, target-affinity change, decreased penetration.
  • Aminoglycoside: AAC / APH / ANT modification, impaired entry, 30S target alteration.
